Chuck Todd opens with the Iran war's arrival on American soil: hackers have hit water systems across multiple states in one of the most serious cyberattacks on U.S. water infrastructure in years and investigators probing an Iranian link. Trump's response tells you everything about the presidency in its current state — he didn't blame the attacker, he blamed the victim, using the hack as an occasion to attack Minnesota Democrats. Chuck’s question hangs over the whole segment: was Trump briefed on the Iranian connection and went after Minnesota anyway? Either way, the first instinct was to find a Democrat to blame, which Chuck calls a kind of polarization disease that leaves a president caring more about his narrative than about American citizens drinking the water. It fits a pattern the episode keeps circling: Jeanine Pirro presented false evidence to a grand jury blaming a former Olympian for damage to the White House reflecting pool, dropped the case when Interior produced documents proving otherwise, and Trump publicly disagreed with dropping it because he still insists it was vandals. Chuck argues negative information never reaches Trump, and people who bring him bad news don't last long — which is how you end up with a president insisting affordability is a Democratic scam
Then, Chuck highlights a Wall Street Journal piece that lays out Trump's corruption — roughly $800 million raised through what amounts to an advertised pay-to-play scheme. Anti-corruption is a devastating midterm message sitting right there for Democrats to pick up… then Chuck Schumer rolled out a bill that Chuck calls a piece of garbage: it wouldn't even cover the conduct in the WSJ story, it's likely unconstitutional because it names individuals, and — most absurdly — it creates a new anti-corruption agency inside the executive branch, meaning a corrupt president would appoint its director and seven board members and, per the Supreme Court, could fire them at will. Congress can already do every bit of the oversight the agency would perform and Schumer's answer to executive corruption is to hand the executive more power and write Congress out of its own job. He closes on Michigan and Wisconsin as the clearest signals of where the Democratic Party is headed — Abdul El-Sayed running a movement inside a Senate race with the explicit goal of changing the party, DSA-endorsed Francesca Wong leading in Wisconsin while the establishment fails to coordinate against her — and on the DSA's new call to abolish the Senate, which Senate Democrats pushed back on without ever defending the institution. Chuck defends it himself: the Senate is a feature, not a bug, a brake on political extremism, and the right response to losing an argument is to win it rather than rewrite the rules.
Finally, Chuck hops into the ToddCast Time Machine to revisit Watergate and Richard Nixon’s resignation, and answers listeners’ questions in the “Ask Chuck” segment.

'Big problems' in confirmation deal Blanche brokered with GOP flagged by experts
sources.text:
The deal Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche appears to have brokered with some Senate GOP holdouts in his confirmation battle may contain a few surprises.
On Monday, reports indicated that Sens. John Cornyn (R-TX) and Thom Tillis (R-NC) were willing to end their holdout and vote to confirm Blanche for the attorney general role after Blanche signed a document attesting that the Justice Department's so-called "anti-weaponization" fund is dead. The $1.776 billion fund sought to pay people who claimed they were wrongfully convicted by the government, and President Donald Trump has said the fund has a lot of support from "big" Trump supporters.
However, the deal that Blanche brokered may not be legally binding, argued Elliot Williams, a CNN legal analyst and former federal prosecutor, on Monday's broadcast of "The Arena."
"It is not clear that any of this is actually binding," Williams said. "And the biggest thing this exposes is the problem with having the president literally be on both sides of the v in the lawsuit here."
The anti-weaponization fund was created as part of a settlement between the DOJ and IRS, two agencies that Trump oversees, in a case involving Trump's leaked tax returns. Williams described the lawsuit as Trump suing Trump, which creates a lot of headaches for judges.
"That creates a huge legal problem that led one of the judges that looked at this to say, 'Wait a second, there isn't even a controversy here. I can't even adjudicate this.' This is a big problem," Williams said.
Kate Beddingfield, a former White House communications director for the Biden administration, added that Blanche's deal also created political vulnerabilities for Trump.
"[This] is actually a pretty significant political vulnerability for Trump," Beddingfield said. "This notion that he is focused on himself, that he is focused on enriching himself and his family. This is actually one of the big liabilities that Trump has out in the country. And one of the reasons that his favorability is so low."
"I also think just the idea that Donald Trump is going to adhere to any kind of independence of the Department of Justice, which he's made very clear he's not interested in, or adhere to any written piece of paper, period, of any kind to constrain him if he decides he wants to move forward with this."

sources.news_title: Did Todd Blanche Actually Kill Trump’s Slush Fund?
sources.text:
Todd Blanche’s path to confirmation as attorney general now appears clear, as the acting AG has officially reached an agreement with the two Republican senators who threatened to withhold their support for him to remain in the role. But what that agreement will mean in practice isn’t yet clear.
Senator John Cornyn of Texas and Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina were reluctant to support Donald Trump’s U.S. attorney general pick due to outstanding issues with the president’s settlement of his unprecedented $10 billion lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. The pair, who both hold a key vote on the Senate Judiciary Committee, objected to the settlement’s creation of a nearly $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund intended to reimburse alleged victims of governmental lawfare and its granting of immunity to Trump and his named associates from IRS audits related to their past conduct.
On Sunday, Blanche indicated he had reached a deal with the senators, issuing an order he says rescinds the Justice Department’s May order creating the fund. “My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions. We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order and update with regard to the May IRS settlement. The Department always welcomes and appreciates productive engagement with all members of Congress,” Blanche wrote.
The order, signed by Blanche, reads, “The Attorney General’s May 18, 2026 Order establishing the Anti-Weaponization Fund (‘Fund’) is rescinded and shall have no force or effect,” adding that it “establishes, beyond any doubt, that there is no Fund.” An accompanying memo, which the acting attorney general did not sign, appears to briefly touch upon the extent of the IRS immunity outlined in the settlement, saying that it “applies by its terms only retroactively” and did not bar any future prosecution and that it would only apply to the named plaintiffs.
Blanche’s overture appeared to satisfy both Cornyn’s and Tillis’s concerns with the pair issuing a joint statement. “We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund. Additionally, the Department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the Treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share,” the senators wrote. “We want to express our gratitude to Mr. Blanche for working with us on this, and we look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon.”
Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa, the Judiciary chairman, quickly scheduled a vote for Blanche’s nomination on Tuesday morning, which would put the acting attorney general on track for a full confirmation vote later this week.
However, questions remain as to whether Blanche’s new deal is enough to render the fund truly dead. As Axios notes, the original IRS settlement stated that it could only be amended “with the written agreement of the Parties,” referring to the IRS, the Justice Department, and the plaintiffs, which include Trump; his eldest sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump; and the Trump Organization. Notably, only Blanche signed on to this new order. Under questioning by Cornyn during his confirmation hearing last month, Blanche conceded that the settlement still stands as written and that it’s an enforceable document Trump could ultimately sue to execute.
Mike Howell, a Republican lawyer who previously sought to be added to the fund’s board, appeared to think the fund could easily be revived. “Can be undone after Tuesday. The Anti-Weaponization Fund is great,” he wrote Sunday.
Trump, who threatened to withdraw Blanche’s nomination until Tillis and Cornyn exit the Senate next year, has defended the fund in recent days and even suggested he would support a bill to establish the fund through Congress.
Democrats in Congress, who remain strongly opposed to Blanche’s nomination, pointed to apparent flaws in the agreement with Cornyn and Tillis. California Senator Adam Schiff wrote on social media that the deal “doesn’t prevent payouts to violent insurrectionists in the future,” alluding to concerns held by many — including Tillis — that people convicted of offenses related to the January 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol could potentially qualify for the fund.
“It doesn’t prevent the admin from bringing the slush fund back from the dead next week or using DOJ’s Judgment Fund for the same illicit purpose. It leaves in place a tax-immunity deal that could help Trump skip taxes on the $2.3 billion he made last year, and still leaves it vague who and what is covered,” Schiff wrote.

Sens. Cornyn, Tillis announce support for Blanche as AG

By Jack Phillips 
Contributing Writer  
Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., on Monday released a joint statement saying they will back acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination to be the next attorney general on a permanent basis.
In a statement, the pair said they struck a deal to end the “anti-weaponization fund” that was set up by Blanche under a settlement between President Donald Trump and the IRS. With their statement, it eliminates a key hurdle in advancing Blanche.
Blanche said over the weekend that he issued an order to end the fund, which the two senators acknowledged.
“We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund,” Monday’s joint statement said. “Additionally, the department has acknowledged in binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS, and the Treasury.”
Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, said that the committee is ready to vote on Blanche’s nomination on Tuesday, praising the acting attorney general as the “right pick” for “our country.”
Previously, the two Republican senators threatened Blanche’s bid to lead the Justice Department over the $1.77 billion fund, which would be used to compensate people who suspect they were unfairly prosecuted by the Department of Justice.
Cornyn and Tillis, who both sit on the Senate Judiciary Committee, had said they would not support Blanche’s nomination without written confirmation that the fund is dead.
On Sunday, Blanche wrote on X that his team “met with committee members and senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions.”
“We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order and update with regard to the May IRS settlement,” he added.
In a statement accompanying the order, the DOJ said that although Blanche had repeatedly advised Congress that the fund was not moving forward and the department had notified district courts that it had been scrapped, the Sunday order “officially rescinds the May 18, 2026, order” that established the fund.
The DOJ said the order also narrows the scope of a separate order issued on May 19 — which gave Trump, his family members, and his affiliates immunity from past tax liability — by stating that it applies “only retroactively.”
“No members were appointed; no funds were transferred; no process for receiving claims was established; no claims were paid. Nevertheless, several frivolous lawsuits have been filed challenging the fund, and at least one court has declined to dismiss those claims as moot,” the order also said. “This order establishes, beyond any doubt, that there is no fund.”
Last month, Blanche was questioned by Cornyn during a Senate confirmation hearing about the fund.
“Has there been a written agreement of the parties to modify the settlement fund?” he asked Blanche in mid-July.
In response, Blanche told the senator: “No, the settlement fund is not moving forward. There is no modification. It never started … it’s not moving forward.”
Blanche, President Donald Trump’s former defense attorney, was named as acting attorney general after former Attorney General Pam Bondi stepped down from the role earlier this year. He had served as deputy attorney general before Bondi left her position.
Cornyn lost his Republican primary after Trump endorsed his GOP opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, earlier this year. Tillis, meanwhile, confirmed in 2025 that he will retire at the end of his term, which ends in January 2027.
The offices of Cornyn and Tillis have not responded to a request for comment on Monday.
Aldgra Fredly contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Cornyn and Tillis Clear Path for Blanche After DOJ Abolishes $1.8 Billion Compensation Fund
sources.text:
Republican Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis agreed to advance Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination after the Justice Department formally eliminated a proposed fund for Trump allies and narrowed a separate tax-audit immunity provision.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche secured the support of two pivotal Republican senators Monday after formally rescinding a proposed $1.8 billion Justice Department fund that could have compensated people claiming they were unfairly prosecuted by the federal government.
Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina said they would vote to advance Blanche’s nomination when the Senate Judiciary Committee considers it Tuesday. The decision resolves an impasse that forced the committee to postpone a previously scheduled vote last week.
Both senators had demanded written assurance that the proposed “Anti-Weaponization Fund” would not be created. Blanche had previously testified that the department would abandon the plan, but Cornyn and Tillis maintained that verbal assurances were insufficient because President Donald Trump continued publicly supporting the concept.
Blanche issued an order Sunday night formally rescinding the May 18, 2026, directive that established the framework for the fund.
“We want to express our gratitude to Mr. Blanche and his staff for working with us on this, and we look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon,” Cornyn and Tillis said in a joint statement.
Their votes are necessary for Blanche to win committee approval and move toward consideration by the full Senate.
The Justice Department said Blanche had repeatedly informed Congress, including while testifying under oath and responding in writing, that the compensation fund would not proceed. Department attorneys had also made the same representation in federal court.
“Although the Acting Attorney General has repeatedly advised Congress through testimony, including under oath, as well as in written responses, that the Fund is not moving forward, and the Department has repeatedly represented to district courts that the Fund is not moving forward, today’s Order officially rescinds the May 18, 2026 Order,” the department said.
The rescission states that the proposed program never became operational following the settlement of Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service.
“No Members were appointed; no funds were transferred; no process for receiving claims was established; no claims were paid,” the order says. “This order establishes, beyond any doubt, that there is no Fund.”
The proposal drew objections from members of both parties because people prosecuted for participating in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, including defendants accused of assaulting police officers, might have been eligible to seek compensation.
Blanche told lawmakers during a June confirmation hearing that the department had no intention of moving forward with the fund. Skeptical senators wanted that position formalized, however, citing concerns that the administration could revive the program without a binding written commitment.
Cornyn and Tillis delayed Blanche’s nomination as several other Republican senators also criticized the compensation proposal. The Judiciary Committee postponed a vote scheduled for Thursday morning after the two holdouts said they needed a stronger response from the administration.
Cornyn said Justice Department officials appeared willing to resolve the disagreement, but the White House initially resisted abandoning the fund.
“I think as far as Blanche and the Department of Justice, we were pretty much on the same page,” Cornyn said Thursday. “But then when the president got wind of it, he wasn’t willing to go along with it.”
Negotiations continued for several weeks as Trump repeatedly defended payments for people he said had been mistreated by the federal government. He also warned that the program could move ahead unless the Senate confirmed Blanche.
After the committee delayed its vote Thursday, Trump said he might withdraw the nomination and submit it again after Cornyn and Tillis leave the Senate next year.
Cornyn lost his reelection bid after Trump endorsed his Republican primary opponent. Tillis is retiring when his term expires in January.
Trump again defended the fund Sunday evening, saying people charged in connection with the Capitol attack had suffered severe personal consequences.
“This would be a reimbursement for the pain that they suffered,” Trump said. “A lot of people like it.”
In addition to abolishing the fund, Blanche’s Sunday order restricted a separate provision of the IRS settlement that had appeared to provide broad protection against tax audits for Trump and members of his family.
The revised language states that the immunity agreement “applies by its terms only retroactively” to claims that were open when the settlement was reached. It does not prevent federal authorities from examining future tax returns filed by the president or his relatives.
Trump’s attorneys notified a federal court Friday that they would appeal a judge’s ruling sharply criticizing the IRS settlement as an improper act of self-dealing.
The judge referred one of Trump’s attorneys for possible disciplinary action and questioned Blanche’s participation in the agreement because he previously represented Trump personally.
Blanche has said he disagrees “with the judge’s insinuations” concerning his conduct.
Justice Department lawyers had already told the court that the compensation fund would not be implemented. They declined, however, when the judge asked Blanche and other administration officials to submit declarations under penalty of perjury promising that no further effort would be made to create it.
Blanche entered the Justice Department last year as deputy attorney general after representing Trump in his criminal cases. Trump elevated him to acting attorney general following Pam Bondi’s dismissal in April.
The president removed Bondi after becoming frustrated by what he viewed as her failure to secure successful prosecutions of his political opponents.
Blanche has since pursued the administration’s priorities from the department’s highest position. Cornyn and Tillis’ decision to support him now places his nomination on course to advance from the Judiciary Committee after the written rescission satisfied their central demand.

sources.text:
Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., have announced that they will support acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, all but assuring victory for President Donald Trump in his bid to install his former personal attorney in the role permanently.
The Monday morning announcement from the senators came just hours after Blanche issued a document that appeared to terminate the Trump administration’s nearly $1.8 billion so-called anti-weaponization fund. The document also clarifies the scope of an agreement the Justice Department brokered between Trump and the IRS not to audit the president, his family or his businesses. The DOJ said the agreement only applies retroactively and to the president, his two eldest sons and the Trump Organization, as opposed to including “related or affiliated individuals” as the order originally stipulated. Those issues had been key sticking points for the senators.
But the legal enforceability of these commitments is ambiguous. It’s not clear whether the document can officially change the terms of the IRS deal because it is not a formal order signed by Blanche. And while Blanche did issue a signed order formally rescinding the fund, the settlement agreement that ordered the creation of the fund remains in effect, and all parties to the original lawsuit, including the president and the IRS, would need to sign off to void it. As long as the settlement agreement remains valid, the government could theoretically revive the fund.
In a statement released Monday morning, the lawmakers said they were “pleased” with the agreement, adding, “We want to express our gratitude to Mr. Blanche and his staff for working with us on this, and we look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon.”
The news virtually guarantees Blanche’s confirmation to lead the DOJ on a permanent basis. The two senators were the key Republican holdouts on the Senate Judiciary Committee to advancing the nominee’s confirmation. Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, was forced to postpone a vote for Blanche’s nomination that was scheduled for last Thursday. That day, Blanche and Cornyn had a closed-door meeting to discuss what it would take for the Texas Republican to support the acting attorney general’s confirmation.
Trump has continued to vigorously defend the “anti-weaponization” fund — both in the court of law and the court of public opinion.
In the Oval Office on Monday afternoon, the president told MS NOW’s Jake Traylor, “These people were treated horribly, and this fund could have given them some solace,” referring to Ashli Babbitt, the Jan. 6 rioter who was fatally shot by a police officer during the attack on the Capitol, and other insurrectionists.

Todd Blanche's AG bid gets major boost as GOP senators end holdout
WASHINGTON – Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's nomination to fill his current role permanently received a major boost as two key Republican senators said they had struck a deal that addressed their concerns over a proposed "anti-weaponization" fund that could have benefited Jan. 6 rioters.
Republican Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who both serve on the Senate Judiciary Committee and are slated to leave the Senate in January, said in a joint statement Aug. 3 they were "pleased" by new statements from Blanche and the Justice Department, and are ready to support his attorney general bid. Blanche clarified limits to President Donald Trump's immunity on tax issues and formally dropped the proposed $1.776 billion fund.
"We want to express our gratitude to Mr. Blanche and his staff for working with us on this, and we look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon," they said.
Blanche posted on social media Aug. 2 a written document stating that a May 18 order creating the fund "is rescinded." Blanche had previously said in testimony to Congress that the DOJ wouldn't moving forward with the fund, which garnered bipartisan backlash when announced from members of Congress concerned that taxpayer funds would go to Trump supporters who were convicted of assaulting police during the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol.
In a separate written document shared in the same Aug. 2 post, Blanche's office said the tax benefits for the Trump family members and business will only apply retroactively to previous tax years, and won't benefit anyone beyond those Trump associates.
Republicans hold a 12-10 majority on the committee. A previous committee vote on Blanche's nomination was delayed after Cornyn and Tillis voiced misgivings about supporting him. Blanche now appears poised to succeed in a new vote scheduled for Aug. 4, setting him up for a vote from the full Senate.
Blanche still needs full Senate support
Following the expected committee vote, a vote by the full Senate is expected to be held before senators leave town for the rest of August.
It was not immediately clear whether Blanche had secured enough support from Republicans to be confirmed with Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky still absent for health reasons. In the case of a tie, Vice President JD Vance is able to cast the deciding vote.
A GOP leadership aide told USA TODAY that Republican leaders are committed to confirming Blanche by the end of the week.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment. The president sidestepped questions in the Oval Office on Aug. 3 about whether he gave Blanche permission to ditch the fund in writing.
"I didn't look at it. All I know is Todd Blanche is great, he's going to do a great job," Trump said of Blanche's statement. "I understand there's been a signoff. I don't know what they agreed."
Judge prohibited Trumps from officially using IRS settlement
The DOJ's settlement, which closed a $10 billion lawsuit the Trumps brought against the IRS after a contractor leaked their tax information, has not only faced congressional scrutiny. It is also being litigated in the courts.

Cornyn and Tillis back Blanche for attorney general after deal on "anti-weaponization" fund
Washington — GOP Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina formally announced their support on Monday for Todd Blanche's nomination for attorney general after reaching a long-sought agreement to end the controversial "anti-weaponization" fund and clarify the scope of a sweeping deal for tax immunity.
"We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund," the Republican senators said in a joint statement. "Additionally, the Department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the Treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share."
The support from Cornyn and Tillis clears a significant hurdle for Blanche in his quest to lead the Justice Department. With their backing, the Senate Judiciary Committee is expected to advance his nomination for attorney general to the full Senate. The committee is scheduled to meet Tuesday morning.
Concerns from the two senators regarding the president's settlement with the IRS in May threatened to derail Blanche's confirmation in recent weeks. The Judiciary Committee had initially scheduled a vote to advance his nomination last Thursday, but the meeting was postponed amid the opposition.
A committee spokesperson said then that the proceeding would be delayed "as work continues to secure sufficient support in committee to favorably report Attorney General-nominee Todd Blanche, who is highly qualified for the job."
Cornyn and Tillis, who are both leaving the Senate early next year, noted in their statement that they have been clear from the outset that "we needed a written document addressing our concerns on the IRS audit agreement and the anti-weaponization fund that included constraining the scope of audit protection by limiting it to the parties of the Settlement Agreement and legally ending the anti-weaponization fund." The pair expressed their gratitude to Blanche and his staff for their work to reach a resolution, and added that they "look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon."
Cornyn told reporters on Capitol Hill that he and Tillis "got a stake driven through the heart of the weaponization fund."
"I think Todd Blanche did what we asked him to do," he said. "It binds not only him but the Department of Justice as a whole, and so I think that satisfies my demands."
Cornyn said it would be a "monumental mistake" for Blanche to attempt to resurrect the $1.8 billion program in another form.
"I can't predict the future so I don't know what somebody might do," he said. "I don't know whether somebody might claim this release as immunity from a future tax audit. But what we wanted to do is make sure that there was an authoritative statement about what the scope was intended to be — that it only affected the parties to the underlying lawsuit."
The $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund was created as part of a settlement agreement Mr. Trump reached with the IRS to resolve a civil lawsuit he filed over the leak of his tax returns by a government contractor. The program would have allowed people who claimed they were victims of "weaponization" by the federal government to seek compensation.
Another provision of the deal granted Mr. Trump, his two older sons, the Trump Organization and affiliated entities sweeping immunity from audits of tax returns.
The terms sparked swift pushback from Republicans and Democrats on Capitol Hill, who were concerned that people convicted for assaulting law enforcement during the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the U.S. Capitol could collect taxpayer-funded payments.
While Blanche told a House committee in June that the Justice Department was not moving forward with the "anti-weaponization" fund, his assertions failed to assuage senators' concerns.
During his confirmation hearing before the Judiciary Committee last month, Cornyn pushed Blanche about the status of the fund and whether Mr. Trump himself had agreed in writing to kill it. The acting attorney general reiterated then that the program is "dead."
Still, Cornyn and Tillis continued to negotiate with the Justice Department to address their concerns about the tax immunity and anti-weaponization program.
After Cornyn and Tillis' opposition threatened to further stall Blanche's confirmation, Mr. Trump delivered an ultimatum over the weekend, telling the GOP holdouts that if their blockade continued, he would keep Blanche on the job as acting attorney general and move to make the Justice Department fund a reality.
Tillis responded to the president's threat on X on Saturday, saying despite the assurances from the administration, Mr. Trump "clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks." The North Carolina Republican said it was "unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal," while adding that he was hopeful the issue could be resolved by Tuesday's committee meeting.
A day later, Blanche announced an order rescinding the Justice Department's fund. In addition to revoking his May directive creating the program, Blanche clarified that the tax immunity extends only to Mr. Trump, his sons Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, and the Trump Organization, and covers only tax returns that had already been filed.
In his announcement, Blanche cited his meetings with members of the Judiciary Committee in recent weeks and efforts to address the senators' concerns.
"We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order and update with regard to the May IRS settlement," Blanche said. "The Department always welcomes and appreciates productive engagement with all members of Congress."
The written settlement reached with Mr. Trump and his lawyers has not been modified.
Mr. Trump continued to defend the "anti-weaponization" fund Monday, telling reporters that it could've given people who claimed they were unfairly targeted by the government "some solace."
"I view that fund as a positive," he said.
Asked whether he signed off on the move to rescind the fund, Mr. Trump said, "I understand there's been a sign-off, but I don't know what they agreed to."
"I think Todd Blanche agreed to reconfirm things that he's already said and what he said was OK," he said.

It’s official: The $1.776 billion anti-weaponization fund is officially, on paper, dead. Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche has been a point of contention between President Donald Trump and the Senate since the day he was appointed acting AG. His chances of becoming the attorney general started off bad, got worse with the controversial IRS settlement, and seemed as recently as this past weekend to be practically hopeless. But then he suddenly turned it all around.
On Sunday, August 2, Blanche announced he had signed an order officially rescinding the fund and narrowing tax audit protections for the president gained in the IRS settlement. Sure enough, a representative of Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX), one of two Republican holdouts on the Judiciary Committee, confirmed an agreement had been reached and that Sens. Cornyn and Thom Tillis (R-NC) now supported Blanche’s confirmation.
Congress: No Carte Blanche for Trump or his AG
The whole Todd Blanche issue goes back a few years. In 2023, Blanche left his law firm to work exclusively as Donald Trump’s lead attorney in a few different criminal cases. He stayed in that role until he was confirmed by the Senate in March 2025 as deputy attorney general. Then AG Pam Bondi got the boot, and Trump appointed Blanche to act in her place.
Senators on both sides of the aisle raised concerns over the man’s loyalties. Could he be counted on to lead an independent DOJ, dedicated to justice rather than a single person’s agenda? It didn’t take long for their fears to seem justified. Blanche was appointed acting AG on April 2 of this year, and by May 18, he had established a $1.776 billion anti-weaponization fund bankrolled by an agreement with the IRS to settle out of court with the president. A day later, he signed an updated deal that permanently barred the IRS from auditing the Trump family or its businesses.
By the time the president nominated him for the actual lead role, Blanche’s chances with the Senate seemed slim. Lame duck senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn – two of the 12 Republicans on the Judiciary Committee – immediately rejected his nomination and threatened to vote against him unless the acting AG formally killed the controversial fund and lifted the audit restrictions.
Of course, Trump and Blanche both seemed unwilling to do that, explicitly on paper, despite both saying that they consider the fund dead. As recently as just this weekend, Liberty Nation News reported on the escalation in the situation – Trump’s threat to pull Blanche’s nomination until January, when Cornyn and Tillis would be replaced – and concluded that it seemed quite unlikely the Trump administration would cave.
Yet here we are.
A New Deal – Exception or Rule?
“My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions,” Blanche said in a statement on Sunday. “We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result, issue the following order and update with regard to the May IRS settlement. The Department always welcomes and appreciates engagement with all members of Congress.”
And so, the $1.776 billion fund “considered dead” by President Trump is now officially dead on paper, and the tax-related protections have been clarified so as to only apply to audits at the time, not any that may come up in the future.
Natalie Yezbick, a spokesperson for Sen. Cornyn, confirmed that the Texas lawmaker is satisfied with the deal and intends to support advancing Blanche to the Senate floor. Sen. Tillis indicated that he would follow Cornyn’s lead.
The committee vote is expected to happen on Tuesday, and now the result seems a foregone conclusion: a 12-10 party-line vote in favor of advancing the nominee for confirmation.
But Blanche and the IRS deal was just one point of contention between Trump and the Senate GOP. So the real question now isn’t whether Blanche becomes the AG – to be fair, that was never really the question at all. As Liberty Nation News explained, the law as it stands allows the deputy to act in the full capacity of the AG during a vacancy indefinitely, so there’s no real reason Trump’s previous plan to withdraw the nomination and try again with a fresh committee wouldn’t work. But this way will ruffle the feathers of fewer senators who, very likely, can easily see themselves in Cornyn’s or Tillis’ shoes and empathize with their position on this matter.
No, the real question now is whether this is the first step in a renewal of the camaraderie between Trump and Republican lawmakers or if it’s just an exception to the conflict and tension that seem to have become the rule of late.

GOP holdouts say they will back Blanche’s attorney general nomination after striking deal over fund
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two Republican senators who threatened to block acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s confirmation to lead the Justice Department said Monday that they will support his nomination, ending an impasse over plans to create a fund to compensate allies of President Donald Trump.
The endorsement from GOP Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis paves the way for the Senate Judiciary Committee to advance Blanche’s nomination on Tuesday after the Justice Department and lawmakers reached a deal to formally rescind the $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” proposed to settle Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service.
Cornyn and Tillis had refused to back Blanche’s bid for the permanent post without official confirmation killing the fund meant to compensate people who believe they were unfairly prosecuted by the Justice Department. Blanche’s written order, issued late Sunday, came after the days of negotiations between the Justice Department and the Republican senators who are leaving Capitol Hill when their terms end in January.
“We want to express our gratitude to Mr. Blanche and his staff for working with us on this, and we look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon,” Cornyn, of Texas, and Tillis, of North Carolina, said in a statement.
DOJ order says ‘beyond any doubt’ that fund is dead
Blanche has repeatedly said that the Justice Department was scrapping plans for the fund, which sparked bipartisan outcry over the possibility that violent rioters who attacked police at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, could be considered for payments. But skeptical lawmakers said they were concerned that could be revived without a commitment in writing, especially because Trump has continued to defend the idea.
In his order posted on social media late Sunday, Blanche wrote that the department was confirming “beyond any doubt, that there is no Fund.”
Since the settlement of the president’s lawsuit against the IRS was announced, “No Members were appointed; no funds were transferred; no process for receiving claims was established; no claims were paid,” the order said. “This order establishes, beyond any doubt, that there is no Fund.”
Cornyn and Tillis had also pressed the Justice Department to limit the scope of a separate piece of the settlement that provided broad immunity for Trump and members of his family from tax audits.
Under the deal, the Justice Department clarified in writing that the tax audit immunity agreement “applies by its terms only retroactively” to claims open at the time of the settlement and does not protect the president from examination of future tax filings. It also makes clear that only the parties that brought the lawsuit — Trump, two of his sons, and the Trump Organization — are covered by the tax agreement.
Cornyn and Tillis said in their statement that they were “pleased” with the concessions made by Blanche.
“From the outset, we were clear that we needed a written document addressing our concerns on the IRS audit agreement and the anti-weaponization fund that included constraining the scope of audit protection by limiting it to the parties of the Settlement Agreement and legally ending the anti-weaponization fund,” they wrote.
Democrats, however, noted that the order rescinding the fund doesn’t stop the Trump administration from compensating Jan. 6 rioters through a previously established process that allows people to file claims for damages if they believed they were wronged by the government.
“This supposed ‘deal’ doesn’t prevent payouts to violent insurrectionists in the future,” Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff said in a social media post. Schiff added that it also “leaves in place a tax-immunity deal that could help Trump skip taxes on the $2.3 billion he made last year, and still leaves it vague who and what is covered.”
Cornyn, Tillis echo GOP colleagues’ concerns as they b
locked Blanche nomination
Blanche’s nomination was thrown into doubt last week after the Judiciary Committee postponed a vote that had been scheduled for Thursday morning as Tillis and Cornyn said they needed more from the administration before they could provide the necessary votes.
After the Thursday vote was delayed, Trump said in a social media post that he might pull Blanche’s nomination and resubmit it after Cornyn and Tillis leave office next year. And on Saturday the president threatened to push forward with the fund if the two Republicans blocked Blanche’s nomination.
On Sunday evening, Trump said that people who had faced charges from the Jan. 6, attack on the Capitol and could have benefited from the fund had “their lives destroyed.”
“This would be a reimbursement for the pain that they suffered,” Trump said. “A lot of people like it.”
Blanche, who served as Trump’s defense lawyer in his criminal cases, entered the Justice Department last year as deputy attorney general. He was elevated to the top post after Pam Bondi was fired in April by Trump, who was frustrated by her failure to successfully prosecute his political enemies.
Though Blanche insisted he wasn’t auditioning for the permanent job, he has moved quickly since taking the reins of the department to promote the Trump administration’s agenda and accelerate investigations into the president’s perceived foes.

GOP senators say they will back Blanche confirmation after he rescinds ‘weaponization’ fund
Reuters//August 3, 2026//
Summary:
- Senators Cornyn and Tillis support Blanche nomination
- Blanche rescinds $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund
- Fund linked to Trump lawsuit over IRS tax records
(Reuters) – Two key Republican senators said on Monday they would support Todd Blanche‘s nomination for U.S. attorney general, paving the way for his confirmation after reaching a deal that would rescind a controversial “anti-weaponization” package that was widely criticized as a slush fund for supporters of President Donald Trump.
Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina had held up Blanche’s nomination as they sought written confirmation that the Justice Department would not move forward with the $1.8-billion fund. Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump now serving as acting attorney general, posted a statement on social media on Sunday saying the fund had been revoked.
“We want to express our gratitude to Mr. Blanche and his staff for working with us on this, and we look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon,” Cornyn and Tillis said in a joint statement.
Their support likely enables the committee to advance Blanche’s nomination on Tuesday. A vote by the full Senate could come as early as Saturday, unless Democrats agree to an earlier vote.
The agreement appears to resolve one of the highest-profile Republican revolts against Trump in Congress, led by two lawmakers who are due to retire at the end of this year.
The fund was created as part of a legal settlement to resolve a $10-billion lawsuit Trump filed against his own government, alleging the Internal Revenue Service had mishandled his tax records.
Supporters say the fund was intended to compensate individuals they argue were unfairly targeted by the federal government. Critics, including Tillis and Cornyn, said it could direct taxpayer money to Trump allies, including those who assaulted police officers during the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot.
PAST TAX CLAIMS
The Republican senators had also objected to a related order that barred the IRS from auditing past tax returns for Trump, his relatives and his companies for any tax returns filed before May 18. They said they wanted clarifications to narrow to whom and how it applied to ensure Trump did not receive blanket tax immunity forever.
Blanche obliged, specifying that it only applies to Trump, his sons and the family business, and that their future tax returns could still be investigated.
“The Department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the Treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share,” Tillis and Cornyn said.
Blanche’s order stated that the tax order “applied by its terms only retroactively.”
Blanche has served as acting attorney general since April, when Trump fired Pam Bondi.

(WASHINGTON) – Under pressure from two Republican senators blocking his confirmation as the next attorney general, Todd Blanche said he is formally rescinding his establishment of President Donald Trump’s so-called “Anti-Weaponization Fund.”
Blanche posted two separate orders on X Sunday night, one rescinding the nearly $1.8 billion fund, as well as another clarifying language regarding the scope of an arrangement that had shielded Trump from facing further IRS audits of his past tax returns.
The move prompted Republican Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, who had been holding up Blanche’s nomination, to announce Monday that they are ready to move forward.
The Senate Judiciary Committee is scheduled to vote on Blanche’s nomination on Tuesday at 9 a.m. Blanche will likely need the support of every Republican on the committee to advance to the floor.
He is expected to be voted out of committee, setting up a final confirmation vote later this week.
“We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund,” Cornyn and Tillis said in a joint statement. “Additionally, the Department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the Treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share.”
“We want to express our gratitude to Mr. Blanche and his staff for working with us on this, and we look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon,” they said.
As part of Trump’s settlement with the IRS in his $10 billion lawsuit against the agency, the DOJ issued an addendum, signed by Blanche in his role as acting attorney general, that would bar the government from continuing any existing audits of tax returns filed by Trump, his family and their companies.
Cornyn said last week that he did need the DOJ to modify the language of the settlement, but that he wants written documentation that the settlement won’t provide tax audit immunity that extends to affiliated organizations for Trump and his family that weren’t part of the lawsuit.
Blanche’s post on Sunday is a signal that he had secured approval from Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, who had been key holdouts on his nomination. The GOP senators had been working behind closed doors and in private talks with Blanche and his team to craft statements they’d find acceptable to alter the language of the controversial settlement.
“Sen. Cornyn has reached an agreement with the Department of Justice, which will be issuing a formal order permanently terminating the anti-weaponization fund and making clear in a binding written document that the scope of the audit settlement is limited to only the plaintiffs, including the President, and the IRS,” Cornyn spokesperson Natalie Yezbick said in a statement late on Sunday.
Some legal experts and even MAGA supporters of the fund, however, have already begun questioning whether it precludes DOJ from giving mass payouts to pro-Trump rioters or the clarification that Cornyn had initially sought to the IRS immunity clause.
The order dealing with IRS immunity notably states that DOJ would interpret the order to mean that it only applies to plaintiffs in Trump and his son’s initial $10 billion lawsuit against the IRS — but that interpretation doesn’t appear to be similarly binding on Trump’s personal lawyers or his family.
And some previous vocal supporters of the so-called “Anti-Weaponization Fund” are already cheering on the language of the order rescinding it — noting that there’s nothing specifically barring DOJ from payouts to pro-Trump supporters who may have attacked police during the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.
Blanche’s orders on Sunday come after Trump floated the possibility of temporarily withdrawing Blanche’s nomination to permanently lead the Department of Justice because of the resistance from the two outgoing Republican senators.
Both senators’ terms will end in January. Cornyn lost a primary battle in Texas earlier this year after Trump endorsed his opponent, Ken Paxton. Tillis announced last year he would not seek reelection after Trump threatened to field primary challengers.
Withdrawing Blanche’s nomination is a decision that would have no consequence in terms of Blanche leading the DOJ.
Blanche can continue to serve as acting attorney general. Acting department officials can serve in the role for 210 days, according to the Federal Vacancies Reform Act — however, that resets if a nomination is withdrawn.
